blocks.text: We are well familiar with various types of waves, such as water waves in the ocean and circular ripples formed on a still pool of water by raindrops. When a musician plucks a guitar string, sound waves are generated in air which reach our ear and produce the sensation of music. The vast energy of the Sun, millions of kilometres away, is transferred to the Earth by light waves. This chapter discusses the formation, propagation and applications of different types of waves.

blocks.title: Wave
blocks.text: A wave is a regular disturbance or variation that carries energy, which spreads out from the source. For example, energy is transferred from the Sun to the Earth in the form of light waves called electromagnetic waves, which can even travel through vacuum. In a medium, however, energy is transferred by regular and repeated disturbances that travel through the medium, making its particles move up and down or back and forth (to and fro).

Imagine a stone thrown into a pond of water (Fig. 7.1): the stone produces a disturbance (ripple) that travels through the water (the medium), and the water particles move up and down at their own places, creating a repeating pattern known as a wave that spreads out. The displacement of a particle of a wave is its distance in a specified direction from its rest or equilibrium position. If the displacement is plotted along the y-axis and the distance in the direction of energy travel along the x-axis, we get a waveform (Fig. 7.2).

blocks.alt: Seen at an angle, circular ripples spread out on a pond from the point where a stone fell in. A red arrow shows energy travelling outward, and a note says the water only moves up and down while the wave travels outward.
blocks.caption: Ripples spreading from a stone thrown into a pond (original diagram after Figure 7.1).

items: Amplitude (A): the maximum displacement of the wave (or particles of the medium) from the equilibrium position.
Frequency (f): the number of oscillations, vibrations or cycles per second.
Wavelength (lambda): the distance between two consecutive similar points on the wave that are in phase.
Period (T): the time taken by the wave to complete one oscillation or cycle; it is the reciprocal of the frequency, T = 1/f.
Speed (v): the speed at which the wave travels. If a wave crest moves one wavelength lambda in one period of oscillation T, the speed is v = lambda/T, and as 1/T = f, v = f lambda ... (7.1).
Phase (theta): the relative position of a point on the wave at a given time.

Top middle: a transverse wave and a longitudinal row of compressions and rarefactions, with the four types of wave. Top right: two waves in phase adding and two in opposite phase cancelling. blocks.long_description: A wave carries energy outward while the particles of the medium only oscillate about their rest positions; its amplitude is the greatest displacement, its wavelength the distance between neighbouring points in phase, its frequency the number of oscillations a second, and its speed the frequency times the wavelength. In a transverse wave the particles move across the direction of travel and in a longitudinal wave along it, in compressions and rarefactions. When waves overlap their displacements add: equal waves in phase give double the displacement, equal waves in opposite phase give none. Two speakers driven by one generator are coherent, so a microphone in front of them finds loud points where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths and quiet points where it is an odd number of half wavelengths. Noise-cancelling headphones play a copy of the noise in opposite phase so that the two cancel.

blocks.caption: Four types of wave
rows: require a physical medium (solid, liquid or gas) to propagate
water waves (ocean, lake, pond ripples), sound waves (audible vibrations in air, water or solids), seismic waves (earthquakes)
do not require a medium, so they can travel through vacuum
radio waves (wireless communication), microwaves (cooking and heating), infrared (heat radiation), visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays (medical imaging), gamma rays (high energy)
associated with particles like electrons and photons
matter waves or particle waves (electron waves in atoms), de Broglie waves, photon waves (light quanta)
propagate along surfaces or interfaces between two media
ocean surface waves (wind-driven waves), seismic surface waves

blocks.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves
blocks.text: There are two main types of wave, transverse and longitudinal (Fig. 7.3). A transverse wave is one in which the vibrations of the particles are at right angles to the direction in which the energy of the wave is travelling. A longitudinal wave is one in which the direction of vibration of the particles is along, or parallel to, the direction in which the energy of the wave is travelling.

blocks.prompt: Distinguish between longitudinal and transverse waves (short question 7.4), and compare the compressions and rarefactions of a longitudinal wave with the crests and troughs of a transverse wave (constructed response 7.3).
blocks.explanation: In a transverse wave the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of energy travel (a wave on a string, light); in a longitudinal wave they vibrate along it (sound in air). Compressions, where the particles are crowded and the pressure is highest, play the part of crests, and rarefactions, where they are spread out and the pressure is lowest, play the part of troughs; in both a wavelength is the distance from one to the next of the same kind.

items: A wave is a regular disturbance carrying energy from a source; in a medium the particles only oscillate (ripples in a pond).

Parameters: amplitude A, frequency f, wavelength lambda, period T = 1/f, speed v = lambda/T = f lambda (7.1), phase. Types: mechanical, electromagnetic, quantum, surface; transverse (vibration across the direction of travel) and longitudinal (along it).
